NEW YORK (CNN) -- Fans of Michael Jackson lined the streets outside Harlem's Apollo Theater on Tuesday for a chance to pay their respects to the late "King of Pop" at the hall that helped launch his career. A hat and glittery glove represent Michael Jackson at the Apollo Theater tribute. The crowd stood eight to 10 abreast in the sun and 80-degree weather for 10 blocks, waiting for hours for a chance to enter the theater. Fans were allowed in 600 at a time, where they lay flowers and other mementos at the foot of the stage and danced to Jackson's music as it played over the sound system. "We left our house at 4 o'clock in the morning and got here at 9, and we were lucky to get here," said Angela Staples, who came to New York from Pennsylvania with her daughter Jasmine. "I'm so happy about the outpouring of love and the crowd and the people. It's so respectful to Michael." Those in the hall observed a moment of silence at 5:26 p.m. -- the time Jackson was pronounced dead Thursday in Los Angeles, California. The cause of the 50-year-old singer's death has not yet been determined. An autopsy on the 50-year-old singer was was inconclusive, leaving authorities waiting on the results of toxicology tests to determine what killed him. Fans have been gathering outside the theater since last week to remember Jackson, who at age 9 won a 1967 Apollo amateur night showcase with his brothers in the group the Jackson 5. "While he went on from the Apollo stage to achieve international fame on an unprecedented level, to us and all of you, he's family because he started out here," said Jonelle Procope, the legendary venue's CEO. Jackson became an idol of both black and white fans and was among the first African-American artists to get widespread play on the music-video channel MTV. But in later years, he was known more for a roller-coaster personal life, including extensive plastic surgery, financial woes and a 1995 trial and acquittal on child-molestation charges. The Rev. Al Sharpton, the New York civil rights activist who became a friend of the Jackson family, urged Jackson's fans not to let critics "scandalize" a groundbreaking performer. "Michael wasn't no freak," Sharpton said. "Michael was a genius. Michael was an innovator. You can't take someone with extraordinary skills, extraordinary talent, and make him an ordinary person. He was extraordinary. He lived extraordinarily, and we love him with an extraordinary passion." The Apollo had been one of the top venues for jazz, gospel and soul artists for decades before the Jacksons' breakthrough.  Sharpton said the theater was home to "the best and the baddest." "You've got to come from the stage of the Apollo and go all over the world to understand Michael," Sharpton said. "We understand his journey, because we were with him every step of the way." The Jackson brothers' amateur night win led to a $1,000 deal for 31 shows at the Apollo, said Bobby Schiffman, whose family owned the theater. "Shortly after their appearance, Diana Ross took them on an NBC special that she did, and there was no looking back after that. They just skyrocketed," Schiffman said. Jackson at the time "was a sweet little boy," he said. "He was extremely talented, extremely easy to get along with," Schiffman said. "He always had a smile on his face, and it was a pleasure to see him working in the theater." CNN's Aspen Steib contributed to this report.

**HARLEM, N.Y. — June 26, 2009**

Under the glowing red marquee of Harlem’s historic Apollo Theater, 125th Street transformed overnight into a sea of tears, silver sequined gloves, and booming basslines. Thousands of grieving yet celebratory fans poured into the streets of Upper Manhattan on Friday to bid farewell to Michael Jackson, who died suddenly on Thursday in Los Angeles at the age of 50.

From the early hours of the morning, the line stretched for blocks down Frederick Douglass Boulevard. Fans of all ages, races, and generations stood shoulder-to-shoulder under the summer sun, united by shock and a shared desire to honor the global superstar at the very venue where his legendary career took flight.

"He belongs to the world, but he started right here," said Marcus Vance, 42, a Brooklyn native dressed in a black fedora and a replica *Thriller* red leather jacket. "The Apollo is where the Jackson 5 won Amateur Night in 1967. Coming here isn't just about mourning a pop star; it's about honoring a piece of our history."

Sound systems mounted on apartment balconies and parked cars blasted "Billie Jean," "Man in the Mirror," and "I Want You Back," prompting massive, spontaneous sing-alongs. Impromptu moonwalkers of varying skill glided across the sidewalk, drawing roars of applause from a crowd determined to remember Jackson’s unmatched artistry.

Directly beneath the Apollo marquee, a massive makeshift memorial grew by the minute. Mourners laid down hundreds of red roses, handwritten letters, vintage vinyl records, and stuffed animals. A framed portrait of a young, smiling Michael from his early Jackson 5 days sat at the center of the shrine, surrounded by flickering prayer candles.

For many in Harlem, Jackson’s passing felt deeply personal. 

"I grew up with him," said Elena Ramirez, 58, wiping away tears from behind oversized sunglasses. "When Michael sang, he spoke to our souls. Seeing that little boy from Gary, Indiana, on this exact stage proved to us back then that Black children could achieve anything. We lost a piece of our youth today."

The Apollo Theater, long a beacon for African American music and culture, lowered its flag to half-staff and dedicated its marquee to the fallen icon. The glowing sign read: *"IN MEMORY OF MICHAEL JACKSON / 1958–2009 / A TRUE APOLLO LEGEND."*

As night fell over Manhattan, the crowd showed no signs of thinning. The glow of hundreds of handheld candles illuminated the pavement, and the immortal chorus of "Beat It" echoed down 125th Street into the humid night air.

Sharpton urged the public to focus on Jackson's unprecedented musical achievements and global humanitarian efforts, calling him an "unmatched trailblazer."

Inside and outside the theater, the day was also steeped in history. Former Apollo owner Bobby Schiffman reflected on the first time he saw the young prodigy perform more than four decades ago.

"He was so small, but the moment that spotlight hit him, he commanded the entire room. To see thousands of people standing here today, decades later, proves that the spark lit right here on 125th Street never truly went out."

As the sun began to dip below the Harlem skyline, the line outside the Apollo showed no signs of shrinking. ---

# SPECIAL EVENT REPORT

**SUBJECT:** Public Tribute and Memorial for Michael Jackson  
**LOCATION:** The Apollo Theater, Harlem, New York City  
**DATE OF EVENT:** Tuesday, June 30, 2009  
**PREPARED FOR:** Cultural & Media History Archives  

---

### 1. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

On June 30, 2009, five days after the sudden passing of Michael Jackson, thousands of fans, community leaders, and public figures gathered at the legendary Apollo Theater in Harlem for a day-long public tribute. Organized jointly by the Apollo Theater and Reverend Al Sharpton’s National Action Network, the event served as a grassroots, community-driven farewell to the "King of Pop." 

While a massive, star-studded memorial would later take place at the Staples Center in Los Angeles, the Apollo event held unique historic and emotional significance, connecting Jackson’s legacy back to the stage where his national career was launched in 1967.

---

### 2. HISTORICAL CONTEXT: THE APOLLO CONNECTION

The choice of the Apollo Theater as a primary memorial site was deeply symbolic:
* **The 1967 Breakthrough:** In August 1967, a nine-year-old Michael Jackson and his brothers (The Jackson 5) won the Apollo’s famous "Amateur Night." This victory caught the attention of music industry executives, directly leading to their signing with Motown Records.
* **Cultural Significance:** Throughout his career, Jackson frequently acknowledged the Apollo as the incubator for Black performing arts that shaped his work. 

---

### 3. EVENT LOGISTICS AND CROWD MANAGEMENT

* **Attendance:** An estimated 3,000 to 5,000 fans lined West 125th Street, with many waiting overnight in hot summer conditions. 
* **Capacity and Operations:** Due to the auditorium’s 1,500-seat capacity, event organizers rotated groups of approximately 600 fans inside every 45 minutes from 2:00 PM to 8:00 PM.
* **Security & City Resources:** The New York City Police Department (NYPD) closed down 125th Street between Frederick Douglass Boulevard and Adam Clayton Powell Jr. Boulevard to manage crowd control and traffic safely.

---

### 4. INSIDE THE THEATER: THE PROGRAM

Inside the auditorium, the atmosphere balanced solemn remembrance with a celebration of Jackson's artistic genius.

* **Stage Design:** The stage featured a single spotlight on a microphone, surrounded by massive floral arrangements. A prominent display included a floral recreation of Jackson’s signature black fedora and white sequined glove.
* **Audio-Visual Tributes:** A continuous loop of historical Jackson 5 and solo Michael Jackson performances played on a large projection screen above the stage, prompting spontaneous sing-alongs from the rotating audience.
* **Key Speakers:**
  * **Rev. Al Sharpton:** Delivered the primary eulogy, framing Jackson not only as a pop icon but as a cultural pioneer who broke racial barriers in television (MTV) and mainstream media, paving the way for Black artists and public figures.
  * **Rep. Charles Rangel:** The longtime Harlem Congressman spoke on Jackson’s global diplomatic impact through music and philanthropy.
  * **Percy Sutton’s Family:** Representatives of the former Manhattan Borough President and Apollo owner recalled the early days of the Jackson 5.
* **Moment of Silence:** At 5:26 PM, a moment of silence was observed inside and outside the theater to honor the musician.

---

### 5. STREET ATMOSPHERE: THE COMMUNITY CELEBRATION

Outside the Apollo, 125th Street transformed into an improvised, high-energy festival celebrating Jackson’s life:
* **Music and Dancing:** Sound systems blasted hits spanning five decades, from "I Want You Back" to "Thriller" and "Smooth Criminal." Impersonators of all ages performed routine choreography on the sidewalk.
* **Public Expressions of Grief:** A makeshift memorial wall of flowers, handwritten notes, stuffed animals, and framed photos covered the facade of the theater. 
* **Global Media Presence:** Hundreds of international news crews broadcasted live from the venue, capturing Harlem as the focal point of worldwide mourning.

---

### 6. CULTURAL AND HISTORICAL SIGNIFICANCE

The Apollo Theater memorial was widely praised for its authenticity and community focus. Key takeaways regarding its impact include:

1. **Reclaiming Roots:** The event reaffirmed Michael Jackson’s deep ties to the African American community and traditional R&B/soul lineage, grounded in Harlem’s history.
2. **Template for Public Mourning:** It demonstrated how community institutions can mobilize quickly to provide a safe, structured space for collective public grieving.
3. **Precursor to Los Angeles Memorial:** It set a celebratory, music-focused tone that influenced the larger global broadcast memorial held in Los Angeles on July 7, 2009.

---

### 7. CONCLUSION

The Michael Jackson memorial at the Apollo Theater stands as a historical moment for Harlem and pop culture history. It brought full circle the career of one of the world's greatest entertainers—bringing him back to the stage where his journey to global stardom began.
